content.summary_of_the_paper:
The core question investigated is how to supplement transformers with domain knowledge, for the pretrain and fine tune.

For pretraining, a new method get proposed -- the topic masked language model, TMLM.

For the fine tuning, the topic subsection matching degree set was created, TSMD.

New models that use TMLM / TSMD have enhancement over base line in the experiment of the paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1) Both the pretraining topic based MLM and fine tuning data seem useful.
2) Experiment gets better metrics than base line model.

Question
1) The best method seems to have unclear conclusion as shown at Table 2. Should the TMLM and TSMD have some conflict in the enhancement? Why some data TMLM or TSMD could get better model than the model with both methods?
2) Do we have eval on an area out of biomedical?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Novelty are mostly at the new task for pretraining and data for fine tune step.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a method which leverages semi-structured document information to design a novel pretraining strategy for creating improved domain-specific BERT models. The use-case in the paper is the following: 1) biomedical domain is the target domain; 2) Wikipedia is used as the knowledge source, relying on the human-designed hierarchy of headings, subheadings, and paragraphs; 3) evaluation is conducted on three biomedical downstream tasks: (i) consumer health QA; (ii) biomedical NLI; (iii) disease NER. Overall, the main improvements are achieved on the consumer health QA task as the new pretraining task is most closely aligned to that application/task.

The main contributions of this paper are:
1) the initiative to use available semi-structured document information and section hierarchy in Wikipedia to improve over the basic MLM objective for pretraining BERT-style models;
2) a knowledge-boosted variant of MLM, termed theme masked language modeling (TMLM)
3) and an automatically constructed large dataset called theme subsection matching degree (TSMD) which is used as another in-domain corpus for in-domain fine-tuning and can be combined with TMLM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strengths of the paper are:
- creative use of Wikipedia's document structure to design new pretraining tasks and datasets for in-domain pretraining and adaptation of BERT-style models.
- some good results on one particular evaluation task: consumer health QA. The results on the other two tasks offer very limited improvements, and with a lack of some straightforward baselines that should have been in the paper, it is really difficult to judge how much the actual proposed methodology would help in the long run (beyond the QA task).

The paper still suffers from several weaknesses:
1. Insufficient coverage of related work and baselines.
- Almost all related work dates back to 2020 or before that, while there has been a large body of work that focused (i) on injecting biomedical knowledge from different knowledge bases (e.g., UMLS) into general BERT-style models, or (ii) combining structural knowledge (e.g., from more general knowledge bases such as DBPedia or WikiData) with distributional-only MLM-style pretraining and fine-tuning. The paper fails to cover many such papers to sufficient detail and it does not compare to such alternatives, e.g., check the following work:
-- https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.04810
-- https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.12716
-- https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.06378 (e.g., this paper combines the use of knowledge graphs to improve QA abilities of general-purpose models and should be used as a baseline)
-- https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11784 (e.g., this paper creates domain-specialised BERT models through contrastive learning strategies)

While some of the work mentioned above can be seen as orthogonal to the initiative/methodology proposed in this work, the paper fails to demonstrate the benefits of their approach compared to previous work, and it fails to demonstrate that their approach might be further combined with such other approaches.

2. The main results mostly show that the more informed pretraining and fine-tuning strategies, as expected, provide improvements over general-purpose or biomedical pretrained LMs. However, as mentioned, there are many other alternatives to infuse domain-specific knowledge into PLMs (see also https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07606, another paper not cited), which should be used as baselines and reference points to clearly demonstrate the benefits of the proposed strategy.

3. The proposed methodology relies on many moving parts (e.g., how to construct the TMSD dataset, the level of masking for TMLM, many hyper-parameters fixed to specific values, score intervals set to a particular interval [-2,2], to name a few), but the ablation study is insufficient and focuses only on the masking aspect. The paper also does not provide sufficient information how all the specific hparams were set.

4. The entire method is very tied to Wikipedia, and it's a pity that it provides evaluation only in the biomedical domain - if the method is indeed general as the authors claim, it should provide evaluation in some other well-defined domain: e.g., I suggest the legal domain and evaluations on some legal tasks: check the LexGLUE benchmark (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00976). This set of experiments would strengthen the 'generalisability claim' of the paper.

5. Some clear omissions from the experiments:
-- Why is only the TMLM variant evaluated on NLI and NER tasks?
-- There are no baselines reported at all for any of the three tasks beyond just vanilla baselines (directly used PLMs)
-- One very relevant baseline is omitted, which are DAPT and TAPT variants that just continue doing standard MLM-ing on in-domain and in-task data, as done by Gururangan et al. in their seminal paper (https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.740.pdf)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- The paper is generally understandable, but the writing can be improved with many too complex sentences as well as odd phrases like "in order to evaluate TDA more scientifically".
- There are some unclear parts on how the actual TSMD dataset has been used: is it tied only to the QA task or can the same dataset be used for more general intermediate fine-tuning oriented towards other tasks? In other words, why hasn't it been used for experiments presented in Table 3?

Quality and Novelty:
- Many concerns on this front (see Weaknesses). 

Reproducibility:
- The authors do not provide a detailed protocol on how they set up their main hyper-parameters (e.g., s0 is just set to -0.6 in 4.2.2 'empirically'. Yet, the method contains many small components that require careful fine-tuning, so replicating the exact scores might be problematic for other researchers.
- The authors do not mention if the results were averaged over multiple random seeds or whether the random seed was controlled at all.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I am not sure, given the weaknesses listed above, that the paper will have a major impact on the field - the results are not strong enough, and the baselines are insufficient and weak, with limited and insufficient coverage of related work. There are also missing details on reproducibility and some unclear aspects of the experimental setup. The paper definitely needs more work, which covers positioning the work, the experimental setup and the presentation front, before it can be reconsidered for publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use semi-structured domain-specific corpus to further pre-train PLMs for domain adaptation. For this, the authors present the Topic Masked Language Model (TMLM) and the Theme Subsection Matching Degree (TSMD) dataset. Experimental results show that TMLM and TSMD improve PLM performance on biomedical QA tasks, and that TMLM improves PLM performance on NER and NLI datasets. The main contribution is they show that pre-training with section label information benefits PLM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The experiments show that the proposed methods benefit PLM in domain-specific tasks. The improvement on QA tasks is significant.

Weaknesses:
- The evaluation is not sound: (1) Most PLMs are evaluated on a benchmark consisting of various tasks and datasets. There are also benchmarks available in biomedicine, including BLURB [1] and BLUE [2]. The authors should evaluate their methods on these benchmarks for better comparison, not on a set of self-chosen ones; (2) The authors only compare their methods with the original PLMs, no state-of-the-art models for the tasks. This is unfair since TMLM and especially TSMD require a lot of engineering. Comparison with other modifications of PLMs should also be done;
- The proposed method is a little trivial, which basically predicts the section label for each passage. The novelty is also limited;
- The pre-training corpus size is also very small - only about 5k articles. The authors should either try to collect more data (e.g., using PubMed) or show that pre-training with 5k articles is enough.

[1] https://microsoft.github.io/BLURB/
[2] https://github.com/ncbi-nlp/BLUE_Benchmark
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Is there any specific reason to distinguish words and tokens throughout the paper?
- The TSMD part is hard to follow - there are too many engineering details. Perhaps the authors can make an overview figure for the pipeline;
- How hard is the pre-training task? Can the authors show the dev set performance (e.g.: PPL or accuracy) of the pre-training task?
- The choices of hyperparameters need to be explained. For example, on page 6, $s_1$ is set as -1.95. How is this value found? What's the hyperparameter selection space and how many selection experiments have you run?
content.summary_of_the_review: The main contribution is the paper shows that pre-training with section label information benefits PLM. However, the proposed method is a little trivial, which basically predicts the section label for each passage. The novelty is also limited. Most importantly, the evaluation is not sound. As a result, I tend to vote for rejection of this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes two techniques to incorporate semistructured information of documents (section/paragraph hierarchies) for BERT training and domain adaptation. The first is theme masked language model (TMLM), which creates topic-passage paired data and performs topic masking during training. The second is theme subsection matching degree (TSMD), which creates a synthetic Q-A like dataset from the semistructured information for BERT training. The paper experiments with these training methods in the biomedical domain using biomedical wikipedia pages. The proposed methods improve performance on tasks such as consumer health QA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The idea of using semistructured information of documents is interesting and well-motivated. Existing language model training methods typically take the plain texts only and then chunk them into smaller segments arbitrarily to feed in the model, which can cause context fragmentation as described by the authors. The use of section/paragraph hierarchies has the potential to mitigate such issues in language model training.
- The proposed techniques and experiments are reasonable. Multiple BERT-style models are studied, e.g., RoBERTa, PubMedBERT 
- Improved task performance is obtained on some tasks such as consumer health QA

Weakness / Suggestion for Improvement
- I think the writing and presentation could be improved. 
    - As a reader, I was a bit confused what “topic” and “domain knowledge” exactly mean in the introduction, and only started to see what they mean later on in Section 3 (e.g. “topic” is basically a concatenation of h1, h2, h3, etc. titles?). It would be great if the authors could define the terminology a bit more clearly in the introduction, possibly using examples or referring to Figure 2, etc.
    - The insight into why topic information helps the learning of domain knowledge (the authors’ claim) could be explained a bit more clearly, in particular in the introduction. Is it because the “topic” (section/paragraph titles) tends to contain biomedical entities deemed useful by humans, and the topic masking technique makes the model learn about these entities better?
    - Figure 2 currently lacks a caption/explanation, and requires the reader to search for a relevant part of the paper that explains Figure 2. I think it would be great if the authors could add a caption that fully explains the topic-passage pairs generation process. It would also be great to explain the meaning of font color, e.g. blue means topic, black means passage.
- The related work discussion is a bit light and is missing relevant references.
    - For example, HTLM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06955) and LinkBERT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15827) are also language models that leverage semistructured information of documents: HTLM uses the HTML representation of documents including section titles; LinkBERT uses the the hyperlink information of documents to gather topically related paragraphs. I think it would be great if the authors could add a bit more discussions in Section 2, e.g. how the authors’ work is complementary to these existing works. 
- I think it would be great if the method could be evaluated on more diverse downstream tasks. For example, biomedical QA tasks like PubMedQA are common benchmarks used in biomedical NLP and are also mentioned by the authors in Section 2, so it would be great to include them in evaluation.
- Accuracy improvement on some tasks like NER looks small (e.g. +0.3%). It would be great if the authors could provide a bit more comments on statistical significance.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity and Quality - I think there is room of improvement here, especially the writing and presentation. Please find my suggestions mentioned in the "Weakness" section above. 
- Novelty - Currently the novelty appears a bit limited. The idea of masking topic-related words seems quite similar to the existing idea of masking entity mentions, etc. in BERT training (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10529), which is actually a reasonable baseline that the authors may want to consider. It would be great if the authors could explain the conceptual novelty and ideally do empirical comparison with the existing topic/entity-aware masking techniques.
- Reproducibility - the experiments and implementation details look reasonable to me. The authors also promise to release the data and code in the introduction section.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed idea of using semi-structured information of documents is interesting and motivated. However, the execution of the paper could be improved, in particular, the clarity in explaining ideas, and discussions about novelty and results.

content.title: Supplementing Domain Knowledge to BERT with Semi-structured Information of Documents
content.TL;DR: A new domain adaptation method is proposed, which emphasize the importance of semi-structured information of documents for BERT capturing domain knowledge.
content.abstract: Adapting BERT on in-domain text corpus is a good way to boost its performance on domain-specific natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Common domain adaptation methods, however, can be deficient in capturing domain knowledge. Meanwhile, the context fragmentation inherent in Transformer-based models also hinders the acquisition of domain knowledge. Given the semi-structural characteristics of documents and their potential for alleviating these problems, we leverage semi-structured information of documents to supplement domain knowledge to BERT. To this end, we propose a topic-based domain adaptation method, which enhances the capture of domain knowledge at various levels of text granularity. Specifically, topic masked language model is designed at the paragraph level for pre-training; topic subsection matching degree dataset is automatically constructed at the subsection level for intermediate fine-tuning. Experiments are conducted over three biomedical NLP tasks across five datasets, and the results highlight the importance of the previously overlooked semi-structured information for domain adaptation. Our method benefits BERT, RoBERTa, BioBERT, and PubMedBERT in nearly all cases and yield significant gains over the topic-related task, question answering, with an average accuracy improvement of 4.8.
